name: Legal fiction as a medieval mode of legitimation
plain_explanation: Medieval rulers and institutions habitually justified new arrangements by claiming continuity with old, legitimate authority rather than admitting innovation -- for example, Charlemagne's argument that the imperial throne was legally 'vacant' (because a woman, Irene, could not be Emperor) rather than simply claiming it by conquest.
precise_definition: Russell's observation that 'the Middle Ages were peculiarly addicted to legal fictions,' using the persistence of formally 'legitimate' claims (however fictional) to mask real shifts in power.
why_it_mattered: It explains how radical changes -- the effective end of Byzantine authority over the West, or the transfer of the imperial title to a Frankish king -- could be presented as continuous with, rather than a break from, established Roman legal order.
historical_origin: Illustrated by Charlemagne's coronation in 800 and, more broadly, by the medieval habit (which Russell revisits in Chapter XI) of parties justifying new institutions through antiquarian or archaistic argument.
examples: Charlemagne's claim that the throne of the Roman Empire was vacant because Irene, a woman, could not legitimately be Emperor
The Donation of Constantine as a legal fiction underpinning the Papal States
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes the same pattern recurs throughout the Middle Ages, for instance in the way twelfth-century parties in the empire-versus-papacy conflict all appealed to supposedly ancient precedent (Chapter XI).
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Fuses political legitimacy with religious sanction (coronation by the Pope).
